maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Because of the importance of the subjects dealt with in this letter I would like to make a statement summarizing the text of the letter and the government's position in regard to them.
The first subject I would like to mention, and which is dealt with in the letter in question, is our tax sharing arrangements with the provinces. Mr. Speaker, this government came into office sharing the view, which at times has been expressed very emphatically by all provincial governments, that the existing arrangements in this field are inadequate. These arrangements, it will be remembered, were made in 1961, for a five year period which ends in March, 1967.
There were, in our view, two ways in which these arrangements needed improvement. First, we felt they did not provide for a proper degree of equalization of provincial revenues from the shared fields. Such equalization is essential if all the provinces are to have not merely the right but the ability to provide a Canadian standard of services in the matters within their jurisdiction.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, at the conference last November it was arranged that a new equalization formula would come into effect for the current financial year. At the same time, at that conference we increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent the federal abatement of succession duties, in order to provide some increase in the share of revenues available to all the provinces.
The effect of these two charges was to cut federal revenues this year by some $87 million. We made it plain at that time that this was as large a change as we could regard as practicable during the year 1964-65. We also made it plain, however, that we recognized the increasing burden that is falling on the provinces because of the cost of the services which it is their constitutional duty to provide to their people. This is especially true of education, and we fully agree with those who say that in the disposition of public revenues as a whole the increasing needs of education merit a very high priority indeed.
At the recent conference in Quebec city, therefore we made, as already indicated to the house, a novel proposal. We suggested that the federal-provincial conference as a body-not the governments separately- should authorize a review of the tax structure in relation to the financial responsibilities of governments and the priorities given to their expenditures. I think this has been recognized as a constructive way in which to handle a most difficult problem, a problem which has faced us in one form or another ever since confederation and which, I suggest, is inherent in the federal nature of our constitution. But, of course, we all recognize that sucn a review will achieve its purpose only if it is thorough and, in particular, if it takes account of the various taxation inquiries which are already under way-and some of them are very near completion- both federally and provincially.
The provincial governments recognize-I would say all of them-the value of this inquiry, but they made it plain that they would like to know how they stand in the meantime pending the completion of this inquiry, and we agreed with that. Therefore, in the light of the discussions in Quebec, the federal cabinet reviewed this matter of tax sharing as we indicated to the conference we would do, and it was decided that we should tell the provinces now what we mean when we say we recognize their increasing needs, especially in the field of education. We mean that under the existing tax sharing arrangements, which have two more years to run after the present fiscal year, we are willing to reduce the federal personal income tax at an accelerated rate.
Arrangements at present provide that the rebate of federal taxes which, of course, creates room for provincial taxes, is 18 per

Dominion-Provincial Relations cent this year and will rise by one point to 19 per cent next year and 20 per cent in the final year. My letter to the provinces which has now been tabled announces that this acceleration will be increased to 3 points a year; that is, the rebate will rise next year not to 19 per cent but to 21 per cent, and in 1966 it will rise further to 24 per cent instead of 20 per cent. There will, of course, be a corresponding increase in equalization payments to the provinces, and these payments will be based on the formula proposed for this year; but the level of taxes to which the formula is applied will be bigger, of course, to the extent I have described. On the basis of current tax yields it is estimated that the increased rebate and higher equalization payments will mean next year a reduction of some $60 million in net federal revenue which will have to be recouped from some other source of taxation.
The detailed figures that I give now are estimates subject to some revision on which work is presently in hand. However, in round figures the extra revenue and equalization payments to individual provinces will be as follows. This is for the year in which this change takes place, the next financial year: Newfoundland, $1.5 million; Prince Edward Island, $300,000; Nova Scotia, $2.4 million; New Brunswick, $2 million; Quebec, $17.6 million; Ontario, $21.2 million; Manitoba, $3 million; Saskatchewan, $3 million; Alberta, somewhat under $4 million; and British Columbia, about $5 million.
That, Mr. Speaker, would be the effect of the extra 2 per cent next year. The further 2 per cent the following year will, of course, have a similar and further effect. I do not need to point out that this further sacrifice of federal revenue from these fields is substantial. Indeed, added to the $87 million for this year which we announced in November and which I have already mentioned, it means that by 1966-67 this government will have reduced its taxes, in favour of the provinces, by more than $200 million a year. We are making that reduction because we believe it is in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. We believe it is the way to serve the priority needs of the country, especially for education.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to turn to another subject which is dealt with in some detail in the letter which has been tabled. It is the subject of pensions. This government came to office almost a year ago with a three point pension program. We thought that the basic old age security pension should be raised to $75 at age 70. We wanted to ensure that this pension could be


available from age 65, on a graduated basis, for those who need it before age 70. Third, we believed that there should be available, in addition to the flat rate pension, a contributory pension related to earnings and sufficient to provide a reasonable minimum of security for all Canadians, and to provide that minimum as soon as possible.
Pensions, as we know, are a field of jurisdiction shared with the provinces under our constitution. We knew as a government that we could achieve a national standard in pensions, which is obviously desirable, only with the agreement of the provinces. We also knew, however, that we could not make early progress in this matter by talking in generalities. Our predecessors, it will be remembered, had raised with the provinces the question of a further constitutional amendment which is required for a plan providing survivor benefits. The province of Quebec had replied at that time, and reasonably enough, that it would want first to know what the pension plan was; and Ontario had meantime proceeded with legislation of its own regulating private pensions. We therefore decided that the way to get progress was to provide a definite basis for discussion with the provinces. We did that last July, and public discussion of various kinds has been under way ever since.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
We could, of course, have done more of the work confidentially and secretly; "in the back room", to borrow a phrase used last week in the legislature at Queen's park by the premier of Ontario. I was glad to note from these remarks of the premier of Ontario that he shared my view that more open methods are better. They enable public opinion to be better informed on the basis of specifics rather than generalities, and public opinion to be brought more fully to bear on the eventual result.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not apologize at all for the fact that this procedure has involved several changes in the details of our proposals. The fundamentals have never changed. We have adjusted the details in a constant attempt to get the best possible pension arrangement which could work for all Canadians.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Trial and error.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Better trial and error than no trial at all.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: This is all error and no trial.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Trial and error and eventual success is better than five years of no attempt.

When Quebec decided to set up its own plan we made some adjustments so that our proposals could operate beside Quebec's. That was in September. In subsequent discussions Ontario expressed some fear about the effect of our proposals on private plans. Accordingly, in January, to meet this and certain other preoccupations of the provinces-we had consulted the provinces about this-we revised our proposals in order to meet this fear as fully as we could without compromising the features of a public plan which we regarded as fundamental.
At the Quebec city conference the government of Quebec made known for the first time to the provinces and to ourselves the details of the plan which it had meantime been preparing. We and the provinces found that it was less different from the federal plan than had at one time seemed likely. That fact, Mr. Speaker, revived in the government the hope that after all we could devise a plan which would meet the requirements of all the provinces, especially in the matter of providing funds for provincial investments, a plan which would still be the same for all Canadians from coast to coast. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, immediately after the Quebec conference I undertook discussions with Quebec to see whether, now that the two plans were before us in detail, we could find one plan which would achieve the purposes of both, and I am very happy to report that we have succeeded.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: This took a good deal of work, patience, understanding and negotiation. The proposal set out in my letter to all the premiers is a proposal in which the government of Quebec concurs. It has been achieved by finding the best common ground in the only two plans before the country, the federal plan and the Quebec plan. There is no question of Quebec accepting our plan or of the federal government accepting Quebec's plan.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh, but the fact is that in our negotiations we have found a common ground between the two plans, and this is how we should work at our negotiations with the provinces. We have found a common ground which takes into consideration certain views expressed by other provinces than Quebec, a common ground which we are confident will appeal to all the other provinces as well.
This means, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am very proud and happy to be able to say this in the House of Commons, that there can now be one pension plan which will be the same
Dominion-Provincial Relations in all of Canada. In Quebec, and in any other province which so wishes, the provincial government can collect the contributions, invest the funds, pay the benefits and administer the plan in that province, but they will be the same contributions and the same benefits everywhere throughout the country. The legitimate rights and interests of the provinces will be met, but the Canadian people's interest in a pension system which is the same wherever they live will be fully served.
That is the proposal that we are now able to put to all the provinces. I believe this is a real achievement which would not have been possible so soon and might not have been possible at all if we had not handled this problem in the way we have, if we had not been prepared to bring public opinion to bear on concrete proposals, not by sitting back talking privately to provinces about something that might be done in the future, which was the procedure followed by my hon. friends. And, Mr. Speaker, if this means putting forward a concrete plan for discussion and then making necessary changes as a result of that discussion to make this plan acceptable to very province in this country, I am quite happy to proceed in that direction.
I am not going to take the time now on the details of these pension proposals which are set out in the letter. I should like to express my appreciation of the co-operation there has been, and my belief that the spirit of co-operation among all the provinces will enable us to bring this matter to a conclusion that will greatly serve the whole of Canada.
May I conclude this reference to the pension plan by quoting, because it is very pertinent to this matter, some remarks made by the premier of Ontario in the legislature at Queen's park last week.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friends opposite applaud the reference to the premier of Ontario in this regard because this is what he said, having been twitted in the house that he was changing his mind on these things, that he was not following a set course, that he was chopping and changing and perhaps even making somersaults. Having been twitted on that score he replied in regard to pensions:
It does not do to take rigid positions. If you do, then you destroy your chance of ever coming up with refinements and changes that in the final analysis will give us a better plan.
Two days earlier, I believe, he also had this to say in the legislature:
Events in the field of pensions have been fast moving for many months. If this latest development can bring us closer in Canada to achieving

Dominion-Provincial Relations a plan national in character, with the best possible benefits for our people containing safeguards to ensure security and a plan which can be approved by all the provinces, then the great efforts and frustrations of the last few months will have been justified.
I commend these very wise words to my hon. friends opposite.
I should like to refer briefly to three other matters that have been dealt with in our recent discussions and which are referred to in the letter which has just been tabled.
The federal government hopes to proceed shortly with legislation providing for the extension of family allowances to children who, either because they are not physically fit to work or because they attend school, remain dependant at the ages of 16 and 17. Because the province of Quebec, which in this respect is unique in our confederation, has an existing program of a similar nature covering the same age categories, these extended allowances will not be paid to Quebec residents. Instead, there will be a compensatory fiscal arrangement similar to that which exists in the case of university grants introduced by my right hon. friends opposite.
In the light of the comments made by provincial governments at the Quebec conference, the federal government intends to propose arrangements whereby guaranteed bank loans for university students would be available in each province up to a defined amount to students designated by such agency as the province authorizes. If any province prefers to rely on its own loan program, it will be able to receive equivalent compensation.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of shared cost programs, the government of Quebec has again indicated that while it wishes to exercise its constitutional jurisdiction, its constitutional right in these fields, it has no intention of dismantling the programs at present provided under cost sharing arrangements. We expect soon to enter into interim arrangements whereby Quebec or any other province-because all the provinces have the same right in this field-may carry out these programs and receive, instead of grants, an equivalent abatement of federal taxes. Longer term arrangements about the programs will be discussed later with the provinces as a whole.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. The government of Quebec, in its discussions with us during the past weeks, has made very clear its firm belief that the wishes of all Canadians can best be fulfilled within a federal structure. The government of Quebec has assured us it is resolutely determined that provincial rights should be exercised, not to the disruption but to the enhancement of the unity of Canada. That
[Mr. Pearson.l

is also our faith and our determination. I am sure it is the faith and determination of all members in this house, and it is shared by all provincial governments. I believe that its validity is demonstrated in what I have been able to announce today. I hope it is a faith and a determination in which we can all go forward, irrespective of political differences in matters less fundamental to the country we are all here to serve.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Prime Minister when he spoke of the unity of Canada and the contribution that the plans now offered will make to that end, I could not but conclude, as he smiled when he said certain things about the planning in the last few days, "Methinks he doth protest too much". As a matter of fact, it is difficult to recognize the views of today as expressed by the Prime Minister and those expressed during the election campaign of which he spoke last evening, when he indicated that while 60 days of decision had been promised, it was really a meaningless promise engendered by the enthusiasm of the election campaign and never meant to be carried into effect. This frank view on his part was in keeping with so many undertakings that were made by the Liberal party.
The record of the government in connection with the promises it made has been that many of these promises have been lost or have strayed. The government cannot pat itself on the back today for what it is doing, because if press reports mean anything this action on the part of the government is as voluntary as I am told shotgun marriages are. He spoke of the leadership that had been given by this government, yet having regard to what we have learned in the last few days the leadership of the Prime Minister and those associated with him consisted of telling the premiers across Canada "Wait for me, fellows; where'er you lead, I shall follow."
I am going to deal in a very general way with what has been said today. I am going to refer to the questions in the order in which the Prime Minister referred to them, first that of dominion-provincial relations. It may be of no significance, but the absence of the Minister of Finance today does not pass unnoticed by the membership of the house. We have made it clear that we will support any action that will assure the provinces of a greater share of the tax dollar so they can carry out their legislative responsibilities under the constitution.
It is well to go back over the years and recall that in 1957 when we assumed the administration of the government of this

country there was a five year agreement in effect with the provinces which provided for the provinces 10 per cent of the personal income tax, 9 per cent of the company income tax and 50 per cent of the succession duties. This agreement had five years to run, but we decided that it represented an injustice to the various provinces. While the agreement still had a lengthy period to run, we introduced legislation to increase the 10 per cent to 13 per cent. Then in 1961 a new agreement was brought into being which provided for a start at 15 per cent, which was to be increased by successive increases of 1 per cent to 20 per cent at the time of the expiry of the agreement.
It is well to review these stages, because it was the Conservative government which took the agreement in existence when we came into office and gave increases which we were in no way required to give to assure that confederation would operate through a proper discharge by the legislatures of their responsibilities.
In so far as the present plan is concerned, it represents a step forward in the direction which we took in two cases, one with an agreement already in effect and thereafter in the new agreement that is now in effect. However, it seems passing strange that all these things have come about in the course of a very few days since the federal-provincial conference, where the premiers not only did not receive hope but many of them left critical of the federal government.
Things have happened during the last few days. We read in the press that the premier of Quebec had expressed himself very definitely as to what he was going to do if the federal government defected. As a matter of interest, I seem to recall that in April 1963, on the Friday just before the general election, the premier of Quebec brought in a budget and at that time stated in effect that unless he got what he expected within a year, things would happen. He is to bring in another budget this Friday.
I would like to have heard these public discussions of which the Prime Minister has spoken in such soulful eloquence. I would like to have been present and to have heard the discussions between them. I am sure if Mr. Lesage could speak with freedom he would be able to tell us of queer sights that have not been seen at any time in the past. It is a strange thing, sir, that only two weeks ago the Prime Minister announced there was going to be an in depth examination by a committee set up by the conference; but now, before the committee has even begun its work, for some reason there is haste and change. The Prime Minister says he does not belong to that school that does not believe
Dominion-Provincial Relations in change. Certainly no one has ever charged him with that and, because of the somersaults he and those associated with him have engaged in within the last few months, nobody ever will.
So far as the fiscal arrangements are concerned, there has been no prior consultation. We have always asked for consultation, which is the essence of confederation, before action is taken. We know that the Minister of Transport, and the chief co-ordinator, visited Quebec. Again we do not know what happened there, but it would be of tremendous interest to have a blow by blow account of that meeting which was marked by so much subsequent agreement.
We shall await the legislation. The extra assistance that is being given to the provinces will naturally bring pleasure to the provinces. It is significant that it is brought in only a couple of days before a provincial election in the province of Saskatchewan. That is another coincidence.
Earlier I mentioned that the Minister of Finance is not in his place in the house. I recall the words of the Prime Minister, and I am sure he recalls them too, which he delivered in Toronto on March 14 last to the district Liberal association, when he said:
But seeing that poor Walter Gordon is going to bring in his budget on Monday, surely we can spare him just a moment ol silent prayer.
Now, sir, I pass on to the last matter, and that is the question of pensions. There has been a tremendous metamorphosis in the pensions system. I recall last July 18 when the Minister of National Health and Welfare introduced her pension plan. It was something the like of which had never been seen before. It was to be accepted as it was. It represented the quintessence of all the wisdom of all the social welfare people of the country. That was the first edition.
We in this party have stood throughout the years for a contributory, universal pension plan for Canadians. First we raised the old age pensions from the degradatory level at which they stood at $46 a month. We raised them immediately we came into office. We not only raised them, but we also had to pay the $6 which the Liberals so begrudgingly gave in the last hours of the St. Laurent administration. Having raised them to a level that at least assured the old age pensioners of some opportunity in life, we then proceeded with the next step to bring into effect a universal, contributory plan.
The Prime Minister tries to brush that aside by saying that we were not able to say what the plan was, and that therefore the province of Quebec would not consent. Well, sir, the only difference between us and them is this,

Dominion-Provincial Relations that we did not present a plan to the provinces. We took the stand that that was our responsibility, but they had a plan which they have had to change, and the one they produced today bears very little resemblance to the one introduced last July, which was subsequently withdrawn, amended and further on reintroduced.
We believe in a plan that is adequate to meet the needs of all Canadians. But what about them? The Prime Minister speaks of consistency. First of all the Minister of National Health and Welfare said all the provinces must participate. Then the Prime Minister said "Well, if Quebec does not come in, we will still go ahead." A little later he said "But if Quebec and Ontario don't come in, it will be very difficult." Then when he concluded that that was to be the case, and he was entirely mistaken so far as Ontario was concerned, he still persisted in the view that even though Ontario and Quebec did not participate we would have a Canada pension plan.
Now, sir, what has happened? Again the veil is drawn. Amidst many luminescent words one thing we have not found out is what happened during the last few days, what happened since the conference, and what discussions took place. The Prime Minister says he believes in open diplomacy. Well, open diplomacy did not apply in connection with the discussions that took place and which resulted in this.
We in the opposition believe that the Quebec plan represented a great advance over the uncertain plan introduced by the federal government. We have taken that stand throughout. It was manifestly superior in many respects, and now the Prime Minister has produced a hybrid plan through the adoption of the Quebec plan, with the necessary modification that must be made of the plan that was previously produced, and that was given to us as though it were the law of the Medes and the Persians.
All we can say of the latest move by the Prime Minister is this. It has brought about the acceptance of principles which the government denied. We said all the provinces should participate. We said it would not be a national plan without such participation. We said Canadian unity would not be served by a plan such as the government had brought in unless changes were made. In this day of the expression "opting out", I can only say that no government in history has ever opted out of more plans and views placed before parliament in this connection in the last few months. A plan is placed before the house and then when there is criticism, with all the strength and unresilience of a reed they produce another. They bend. They opt out of

what they previously declared to be essential features of a national plan. We had a plan embodied in the original bill. It was withdrawn and replaced by another; then withdrawn and replaced again. Yet the Prime Minister rises today after such an inept and bungling performance and says "Look at me." Consistency is not a jewel. But what parliament is entitled to have is a government plan, as was placed before parliament, not a series of plans dictated to it following the introduction of the first. There should have been consultation in advance and only then, after consultation, should the measure have been introduced.
As far as this plan is concerned, we have always been in favour of a national contributory plan and we shall continue to be in favour of such a plan. We think the present one, even in its latter form, is a better one than the government produced and placed before the house. We think, however, particularly as the government has said this is a much better plan than the one they previously had, that after this bill is introduced into the house it should have an early transfer to a committee of the house for further investigation, examination and improvement. That is our view. When I said "committee of the house" I meant to say a joint committee of both houses. We feel that such a committee is more necessary now than ever because we have before us a government which has already brought in one plan with fife and trumpet as if it were the greatest thing ever. Now they have retreated. They have retreated from the things they stood for, having tacitly admitted that their plans have been proven ineffective and inoperative and would have been a denial of Canadian unity.
We say that the bill now to be introduced- the summum bonum, as it were, of the collection of monstrosities which have already been before the house-should go before a committee. We shall give our support on the question of principle and we shall do our best to bring about any further changes which are necessary to ensure that Canadians in every part of the country may have the opportunity to benefit from a contributory pension in addition to a fair basic pension which has been adopted as part and parcel of the social security law of our country.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has made a statement to the house on four matters on each of which I should like to comment very briefly.
The first statement had to do with increased revenue to the provinces. I think that announcement will be welcomed by all members of the house and by the provinces of

Canada, because the provinces have been facing an increasing demand for services in those fields which come under their jurisdiction. This has been particularly true with reference to education and the need for hospital accommodation, health services, welfare, and municipal services in respect of which municipal governments are looking increasingly to the provincial governments, and the provincial governments have reached the point where they can no longer assist the municipalities in the absence of some further sources of revenue.
Last fall the government made its first move in this direction by allocating an additional $87 million to become effective in this fiscal year, but it should be remembered that about half of that amount was given to one province, so the balance would not amount to a great deal when scattered over the other nine provinces. The Prime Minister announced today that the provinces are to be given an additional 2 per cent in personal income tax abatement commencing January 1,	1965, and
another 2 per cent abatement commencing January 1, 1966. This will give the provinces very welcome relief in enabling them to find resources to meet their increasing responsibilities. It will certainly help. But I think we should not delude ourselves into thinking that the basic problem facing the provinces as they try to meet their legitimate responsibilities under our constitution does not still loom very large; a far more fundamental approach will have to be taken in order to solve it.
The second statement which the Prime Minister made has to do with the Canada pension plan and, as hon. members know, this is the third plan which has been outlined in this parliament. I make no mention of the plan outlined by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on January 30, 1962 on a national hook-up, which I take to have been largely Liberal political window dressing not meant seriously as a plan for the people of Canada. But this is the third plan which has been before this house, and I do not quarrel with that. I still think that the plan which was submitted on July 18 last gave the participants greater benefits for the money they were to contribute than any plan which has been submitted since. However, that plan ran into difficulties. Some of the provincial premiers were concerned about the need for investment funds; and well they might, because the provinces have a serious problem in finding adequate funds both for resource development and for social capital.
Personally I do not favour looking to pension funds as a means of finding this capital. I think there are better and more equitable ways of finding investment capital. I
20,	1964
Dominion-Provincial Relations think to use pension funds for investment purposes confronts the provinces or a federal government with two problems. The first is that the burden of raising those funds falls on the lower and middle income groups and this is not the place where we ought to be levying money for investment purposes. Second, I think there is a conflict of interest between those who want to use pension funds for industrial development and those who are concerned about protecting the investment of the beneficiaries. The latter have to be cautious and careful, while those who are thinking in terms of economic expansion have to be prepared to take some risks.
This is a conflict of interest which I think would seriously hamper the free use of pension funds for industrial development. I think the answer lies in having the federal government proceed to establish a Canada development fund to supply the necessary capital to industries and to the provinces for resource development. I still express my great regret that this has been dropped into the dustbin of history. The federal government also needs to make available to the provinces large sums of money for social capital. Had these two things been done, then the premiers would not have had to think of the pension fund as a source of investment. But, Mr. Speaker, this house and the people of Canada have to concern themselves, not with the kind of pension plan we want but the kind of pension plan we can get, and the Prime Minister has now put before us a plan that it seems is generally acceptable to all the provinces of Canada.
I would like to know more about the negotiations. I was surprised that the negotiations seem to have been carried on mainly by Mr. Kent of the Prime Minister's office and the Minister of Forestry, and there seems to have been a complete disappearance of both the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance, whom I thought would have been generally concerned with this problem. But whatever the discussions back of this plan, we now have a brief outline of a plan which we will have an opportunity of examining in greater detail.
We in this group have insisted all along that a contributory pension plan should have three basic principles; that it should be universal in coverage, that it should have portability, and that it should be on a pay as you go basis so that it would give the greatest possible benefits for the smallest possible contribution. In the plan which the Prime Minister has outlined the first two principles, and by far the most important principles, have been saved and an additional principle has been added; that is, that the federal government has been able to secure

Dominion-Provincial Relations from the provinces their acceptance of a constitutional amendment which will enable the government to include in the pension plan survivor benefits.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this plan contains the best features of the Quebec plan and is a great improvement on the plan which is now before the house. I think this proposal which the Prime Minister has outlined very briefly represents a real victory for national unity and for common sense.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think we should waste the time of the house by trying to take credit on the one hand for all the virtues of the plan that has been evolved, or trying on the other hand to belittle the accomplishment that has been achieved. I think we should take pride in the fact that the federal and provincial governments of Canada have now taken a great step forward, and that this could be a red letter day in the history of social welfare in Canada, if it is the first step toward providing the people of Canada with a universal, portable contributory pension plan.
The Prime Minister has also outlined a proposal for extending family allowances to those in the 16 and 17 year old groups. This will apply to all parts of Canada, but in view of the fact that the province of Quebec already provides this service they will receive financial compensation for whatever outlay they make. I think this is a happy solution, in that it will give to the young people in this age group who are still attending school benefits all across Canada, will continue them in the province of Quebec, and will compensate the province of Quebec for its financial outlay.
With reference to the student loans, the Prime Minister's statement that the provinces will be allowed to administer these if they so choose and receive equivalent compensation seems to me to make sense, in that the provinces are in a good position to administer student loans because they are familiar with the students' problems. It will create some problem with regard to students moving from one part of Canada to another. Also I hope this will be kept in mind when the 10,000 scholarships are granted which the Liberal party promised before the election.
The point I want to make in closing, Mr. Speaker, is that the statements made by the Prime Minister today indicate very clearly that if we want to advance in Canada, if we want to make progress in reaching new social and economic plateaus, we will have to be flexible, we will have to recognize that experiment is the price of growth; and we will


have to adjust ourselves and develop new techniques to meet the problems of confederation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: There is a price which Canada cannot afford to pay for national unity. That price is to emasculate the federal government of all the powers which it needs to promote economic growth and full employment. But, happily, today no such price is being asked, and with regard to the proposals which the Prime Minister has made, I believe that the price is one which we can afford to pay and which we should pay gladly.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable interest that we have followed the reports of the negotiations which have been taking place the last several days, and now to hear the Prime Minister speak as he has spoken regarding the most recent developments relating to the fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the matter of pensions. I think perhaps the outstanding aspect of the decisions and policies which have been announced this afternoon does not relate directly so much to the pension plan, nor to the fiscal arrangements, as it does to the unity of our country.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Somehow I seem to sense that we have passed over what was shaping up to a very serious crisis. Perhaps as in the days ahead we look back at this point, we will see that this is exactly what has happened. Premier Robarts of Ontario foresaw this when he stated at the federal-provincial conference, as is referred to in the letter which the Prime Minister has sent to the provinces, that it is important to the unity of the country that our pension arrangements across the country should not set up obstacles to the movement of the people and therefore must be national in character. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the Prime Minister when he says these decisions will help to unify our country.
The arrangements regarding the relinquishing by the government of further financial concessions is a recognition by the government that the provinces have not been getting their fair share of Canada's tax dollar. The acceleration of the rate of return of the income tax dollar appears to me to be founded upon the Diefenbaker-Sauve arrangements that were established in 1959, and this is good.
This being so, we must not consider it a final solution to the problem. A permanent and definite agreement must be reached for a just and all-inclusive arrangement which defines federal and provincial areas of rights

and responsibilities. This very definitely concerns provincial autonomy, and I think this can well be the second step which must be taken to further develop this point of unity which we have just mentioned.
In this regard I think it is good to note that all that comes out of Quebec is not negative. In fact there can be no doubt that if the present pension plan which has been referred to today can go forward to materialization, all the provinces are going to benefit as a result of the lead which has been taken in formulating a specific plan by the province of Quebec.
There is nothing wrong in taking a second look at a problem. I think it is commendable that we can lay down what we believe to be the correct plan at the time and then be able to adjust it as we realize more fully all the implications which are involved. I think as this pension plan and these fiscal arrangements are discussed further by the provinces, in this house and in the committee to which they will be referred, it may be necessary in some minor points to take still further looks at it. But at least we have reached at this point of the development of a national pension plan something which is certainly more hopeful than we have had thus far.
The result of last week's negotiations between the federal and provincial governments has proved without doubt that the position of the provinces is becoming stronger, and that the need for a continuing negotiation organization and consultation body is necessary between our different levels of government. I trust that this will lead very quickly to the setting up of some form of federal-provincial affairs department.
From what we have heard today the federal government is obviously pleased with the arrangements which they have been able to make, and I gather from reports that the provinces are likewise pleased. However, the person I am most concerned with is John Citizen, because during these past weeks of negotiation I do not think he has been consulted too much. Certainly this is a far different plan from what he has heard about before. The original plan was for a pay as you go plan. That plan meant that this generation supported today's senior citizens, and that when today's workers were retired they would be supported in turn by the workers of tomorrow. That would have meant that we could quickly look after one age group in immediate need at the present time, those between the ages of 65 and 70, and do so without waiting very long for the plan to get started. It would also mean that we would avoid the depressing long term effects of accumulating large reserves and plunging the whole country into debt by investing them.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
This brings me to the point that a pension plan should be intended basically to provide pensions for the people and to provide the portability which is not available to them at the present time. There is the fact that there is now being added to this pension plan a source of funded capital, although it is being left with the provincial governments for their use, which is doing something beyond which I think a pension plan perhaps should go. I sympathize with the provincial governments because we all know they need money for development, but money for development should not be confused with money for pensions. However, I do not feel that the financial needs of our provinces and of our municipal governments mix too well together in this question of pensions. I just remind the house in this regard that we have our own Bank of Canada, and there is no reason why our needs for capital development within the provinces and municipalities could not be supplied therefrom.
However, this is not the time for debate on the pension plan. I would just point out that there are many matters which will have to be discussed when the proposed legislation is referred to committee, and there will likewise be discussions between the provinces as well. It is also good to note that there are survival benefits being planned. I am a little concerned that the self employed are going to be responsible both for the employer's contribution as well as the employee's contribution. With regard to the latter remarks of the Prime Minister, it is also good to note that all our student bodies across the country will be able to benefit equally. All these matters add up to the sum total that it is our opinion that progress has been made, and we look forward to the continuation of this debate.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that having been told of the new developments at a few minutes' notice, we are unable to delve properly into the matter. Yet, at first sight I shall not hesitate to say that, even if this is not quite satisfactory, the situation as a whole is rather gratifying.
Mr. Speaker, our group has now been sitting in the federal parliament for two years, and this is the first time that we see a government, whether the present or the last one, take concrete action to promote better understanding between the provincial and federal governments, or between the two great nations which make up this country.
Mr. Speaker, I must therefore say that as there had been no action on the part of the governments for the last two years, we began to feel slightly discouraged about future developments in the house. Yet, today's gesture

Dominion-Provincial Relations will encourage us to claim twice as loud as before, since we realize that, when we raise our voices to expound what we believe to be our rights, we get some satisfaction. Consequently, we shall clamour twice as loudly, in order to obtain twice as quickly the true confederation of two nations where each will have its recognized rights and responsibilities.
The pension scheme which has been explained today is, I think, a concrete example thereof. Understanding has been reached along general lines; there has also been agreement on the percentages to be levied and on the amounts to be paid to beneficiaries.
However, nothing prevents thereafter everyone from keeping his jurisdiction, from administering and operating his own pension plan; the province of Quebec will keep on administering hers, while the nine other provinces, if they wish, will agree to leave that jurisdiction with Ottawa or they might decide to administer their own pension plan, if they so desire.
In other words, there is agreement on the terms, but everyone is the master of his own fate as far as the pension plan is concerned according to the announcement made today. That is exactly what we understand by a true confederation of two nations, where there is room for agreement, but where everyone continues to guide and work out his own destiny as he sees fit.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to income tax, I must say that it is a little less satisfactory. We asked for 25 per cent, we got 24 per cent; we are short 1 per cent. I admit that the goal has almost been reached. The Prime Minister certainly showed himself a clever diplomat in coming to terms with the premier of Quebec-within 1 per cent.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext: In two years.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING TAX SHARING, PENSION PLAN, ETC.
speechtext:
I wanted to come to that; in two years only, whereas it should have been done before the budget was brought down in the Quebec legislature.
Of course, things will go faster because the income tax rebate granted to the provincial governments will increase by 2 per cent, then 3 per cent each year.
Mr. Speaker, some people may feel that things are not going fast enough considering that it has taken years-in fact, since the war-to get to those 24 per cent, considering also that from year to year or at least every two or three years, the rebate will be multiplied not mathematically but geometrically since it is being increased threefold today. However, I feel that this proportion of 24 instead of 25 per cent will be considered satisfactory by those who wish to find a fair solution through understanding and harmony. However, this is not a final agreement but

rather the beginning of negotiations which will end only the day that Quebec has recovered 100 per cent of personal and corporation income taxes and of the estate tax.
In my opinion, this will be possible in 1967, when the provinces will be able to put an end to the agreements and get 100 per cent of the income tax.
As for the pension plan, the federal government has deemed it advisable to change its mind; I do not think it is a mistake. There is a latin proverb which says:	Errare
humanum est, it is in the nature of man to make mistakes. Well, I believe that the federal government has at least gained a point; the provincial government wanted to increase income tax by 4 per cent for the pension plan, now it will be increased by 3 per cent only. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said a moment ago, I do not think that a pension plan should be used to accumulate savings for reinvestment in industry. In my opinion, a pension plan should serve to give bigger pensions to those who have reached retiring age. Above all, let us not forget that those who will have to subscribe to the pension plan at the rate of 3 per cent later on will borrow their own money so as to be able to develop. It might be better to leave them their money now, so that they might prosper without having to borrow later from the pension fund.
With regard to the $10 paid to students, the young people in the province of Quebec will be passed over without being able to benefit therefrom. On the allegation that they already benefit from this amount, the whole sum will be paid out to the provincial government. Now, there have been some instances in the past where things were not done in that way. For instance, when the old age pensions were increased in Alberta and British Columbia, the amount was larger than in the other provinces, because those two provinces were granting an additional amount to their senior citizens.
When old age pensions were increased, those two provinces did not tell the federal government: "Hand that money over to us, so that our old people will get neither more nor less, but certainly not less, than in the other provinces." Nobody tried to reduce what the provincial government was already paying out, so that the federal increase would be of no use to anybody.
I wonder why the premier of the province of Quebec would not rather undertake to pay those additional $10 to the young people in the province so that they would get $20 as a school allowance. They have great need thereof, as until now education in the province of Quebec has proved almost a failure,

and education is certainly not free, because taxes have increased and students have to pay still more than formerly, in order to be able to continue their studies at the university level.
In concluding I should like to refer to a sentence which went by very quickly in the statement made by the Prime Minister. He said that the federal government will have to recover that from other sources of income, in reference to the additional tax rebate of 2 per cent per year. Does this mean that the federal government intends to increase taxes or to do in Ottawa what Mr. Lesage was going to do in Quebec, namely impose double taxation? A warning must be given to this government which shares the tax yields to the benefit of the provinces, that it should not attempt to get more income out of the pockets of the taxpayers already overburdened with taxes.
One last remark, Mr. Speaker, especially as regards the province of Quebec. A year ago, the premier of that province asked for a tax rebate equivalent to $150 million and said that he would need that amount this year. In November, he received an amount of some $43 million. For next year, he will get $17 million more, that is $60 million, while Quebec requirements are of $150 million.
Mr. Speaker, I think that is the crux of the statement made today. In giving back to Quebec the revenues to which it is entitled under the constitution of this country, and also because of its priority requirements, I believe that the federal government does not go far enough and I wish to warn them that if they do not go farther than they did today, there is a risk that the dissatisfaction of the province of Quebec will not die out with the crumbs it got today, but will rather become more pronounced, because Quebec, wishing to be in a position to develop itself and be the master of its own destiny, is eager to have complete restitution of its revenues.
The sentiments prevailing at the present time in the province of Quebec will not be stifled by the few crumbs that have been handed out today. To do it successfully would require the complete return of its income. It may be possible to make the province wait a while longer by gradually giving back to it part of its revenues, but I feel it will have to be done at a much faster pace than the one mentioned today.
That will have to be done, not by handing out a few crumbs now and then, but by proceeding at such a pace that, within a few years at the most, Quebec will have recovered all its sources of income.

Mr. Speaker, for a beginning, perhaps that is not much, but at least it is something. More must be done and at an accelerated pace. Should that be the case, confederation, renovated by the adoption of new principles, will be able to survive and good understanding will prevail between our two great nations, both living in harmony in one great country called Canada, providing we proceed right now, at as fast a pace as the rate of growth and as fast as necessary to give satisfaction to Quebec which, after all, is only claiming the rights granted to her by the constitution of 1867.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the second report of the special committee on procedure and organization, presented on April 15, be now concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my gratitude to the special committee on procedure and organization for according me the honour of moving concurrence in that committee's second report. I am grateful, too, to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for his consent to be the seconder of the motion. Speaking both for the member for Peace River and for myself, I may say that we are doing this on behalf of the special committee on procedure and organization.
Hon. members are aware that the second report, concurrence in which we are now asking, is to be found on pages 211 to 214 of Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday, April 15. Hon. members are aware also that in that report it is made clear that the two main recommendations which the committee is now making to the house are made on a trial basis. If this report is concurred in, as we hope it will be, the proposals contained in it will come into effect today and remain in effect for a period of six weeks or until the end of the month of May, at which time it will be for the house to decide whether or not these proposals are to be continued.
The report makes it clear also that although we are today presenting only two main proposals, this is only the beginning of our work. The committee hopes to bring in other changes from time to time pending a final report on behalf of the committee. I draw hon. members' attention to the fact that there are two main sections of the report now before us, concurrence in which is now being sought. The first section relates to the orders of the day question period, and the

Procedure Committee second section relates to the handling of notices of motions for the production of papers. Because the second of these proposals is the least complicated I should like to deal with these two proposals in reverse order.
With regard to notices of motions for the production of papers, we are making two suggestions. The first one we make by an amendment to a standing order, and it is to the effect that there should be a time limit on the total amount of debate that might take place on a notice of motion for the production of papers that has been transfered for debate on every second Thursday at five o'clock. We propose that when a motion under that order has been debated for a total time of two hours and thirty minutes, the debate shall be interrupted and the minister, whether or not he has already spoken, shall be given five minutes at that point and the mover of the motion five minutes, whereupon the question shall be put.
The other suggestion we make with regard to notices of motions for the production of papers has to do with the way in which they are handled in the first instance, when they are called on Wesdnesdays. We suggest that they be handled in a manner similar to that which is now employed with respect to the printed questions on the order paper. I need not go into details about this. I am sure all hon. members will realize that a good deal of time can be saved in this way and, as a matter of fact, certain annoyances we are now experiencing on Wednesday afternoon, could be avoided. I trust that the proposals we have made with respect to notices of motions for the production of papers will commend themselves to the house and that they will be accepted for this trial period between now and the end of the month of May.
I return to the first of the two main sections of our report, namely the section that has to do with the orders of the day question period. In legal or procedural terms, we have not had any such period up to the present time. There is nothing in the standing orders that provides for questions prior to orders of the day, but tradition has overridden the standing orders and it is the view of the committee that we should now regularize this procedure by a standing order and should make certain provisions regarding it.
We considered very thoroughly and very seriously, the proposals that have been made to put a time limit on the orders of the day question period. We have decided, both as a subcommittee and as a main committee, not to recommend a time limit except for the fact we do recommend trying a 30-minute time limit on Wednesdays only. The reason we do not propose a time limit on the question period

is that we feel there are too many complexities. In view of the number of parties there are in the house; in view of the questions of order and points of privilege that arise, we feel we might be asking for more trouble than we would get rid of by applying a time limit. We felt rather that we should approach this orders of the day question period from two points of view. We feel that, on the one hand, there should be some clearcut rules and directions for the orders of the day question period and, on the other hand, there should be a recourse, an escape valve or an alternative that would make it possible for Mr. Speaker with the co-operation and assistance of the house, to apply the rules and directions that we suggest for the orders of the day question period.
Having these two things in mind, we therefore recommend a standing order to regularize the orders of the day question period and to give control over that question period into the hands of Mr. Speaker. In addition to the standing order, we recommend, as our report indicates, that certain guide lines should be followed in allowing questions during this period of time. We hope that this standing order and these guide lines will enable the house, under the direction of Mr. Speaker, to improve the orders of the day question period. We hope it will shorten it, but we want to make it clear that that is not our only concern. We would like to see the period sharpened and made the effective part of our parliamentary procedure that the question period ought to be.
It is our very strong view, Mr. Speaker, that merely to impose restrictions on the orders of the day question period, by itself, would not solve the problem and would not retain the rights that are inherent in the asking of questions. We therefore propose, and members are familiar with it now, that on three nights in the week, Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, there be available a possible half hour period during which there might be short submissions on three different subjects on each of these three nights.
Our proposal is that if during the question period a member feels dissatisfied with the answer he gets from the government or if he feels dissatisfied with the direction given him by Mr. Speaker not to proceed with his question, he may give notice that he wishes to raise that matter at the time of adjournment. He can give that notice orally at that moment if he wishes to do so. But whether or not he gives it orally, we direct that he give it in writing to Mr. Speaker by five o'clock and we direct that at six o'clock Mr. Speaker indicate-that is on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays-what matters will be allowed for debate that evening. We lay down

certain matters that Mr. Speaker may have regard to. We hope we have covered most of the details to make this a workable operation.
One of the conditions we suggest is that consideration be given to apportioning the opportunities among the various parties in the house. We feel that when the plan is put into operation, we can shorten the time taken for the question period and yet preserve the right of members to have a chance to say something on matters that they feel are not satisfactorily dealt with in the question period.
These three possible statements or debates at night, between ten o'clock and 10.30, will be limited absolutely to a total of ten minutes each, seven minutes for the member who has been given the floor, and three minutes for the minister or parliamentary secretary who may wish to reply. We also provide that if any one of these matters takes less than ten minutes then the house gains, in the sense that it adjourns that much earlier.
As I have indicated to hon. members, the details of this arrangement are spelled out in the report which is to be found in last Wednesday's Votes and Proceedings. We feel if hon. members will give this whole proposal a fair trial and will co-operate with Mr. Speaker, we can perhaps institute a new approach, a new attitude toward the question period, from which we will all benefit.
Mr. Speaker, I make this motion on behalf of the committee. I present it to parliament as a whole on behalf of parliament as a whole, but I do crave a moment to introduce just one personal note, and I shall put it this way. Although I am doing this on behalf of the committee, it is a fact that I sit on the opposition side of the house, as I have all my parliamentary life. Thus I have a built-in desire to protect the rights of the opposition, to protect the rights of individual members in the question period, and yet it is precisely from that point of view that I want to say that I feel this new arrangement that we are proposing not only will help to shorten the question period but will protect those rights by helping to sharpen the question period and make it a more effective instrument in the course of our parliamentary procedure.
We welcome the interest shown in the report by the news coverage given to it during the last several days. We welcome the editorial support we have noted in various newspapers throughout the country. I welcome the support hon. members in all parties have indicated, in speaking to me personally about it.
Procedure Committee
I hope we can therefore adopt this on a trial basis, and that the house will support Mr. Speaker in applying the rules and suggestions we have laid down so that, all told, we can take a step forward. With respect to the rules and recommendations about the question period I would like to make this one further point. Up to this time, when Mr. Speaker has sought to apply rules and precedents about the question period he has had to rely on what former speakers have said, but these have not been dicta that came from the house itself. If the house today passes this report, Mr. Speaker will have as his authority not just statements from the Chair, statements out of the past, not just his own judgment, but he will have the direction of this very House of Commons which we will have given by supporting this report at this time.
So, Mr. Speaker, believing that this will be a useful step forward in our attempt to improve the procedures of the House of Commons, I express the hope that the house will support the motion for the adoption of this report; that it will support the letter of it, that it will support the spirit of it, and that from this day forward our question period and some of our other procedures in the house may become, even more so than they have been, an expression of the best traditions of parliamentary procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as might be thought at this time I would like to say a few words on this particular subject because I have, shall we say, a built in or vested interest. I think hon. members will realize my own interest in the question period.
In making a few brief comments I would like to say that I too share the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which I believe were fairly general in the committee. However, it must be clearly pointed out that the adjournment period that is proposed under standing order 39-A must not be deemed an opportunity for an extension of government business in that at five minutes to ten o'clock, or at ten minutes to ten in the evening it would not be suddenly put to the house: How about waiving the adjournment debate and carrying on with the government business?
We will see how this works, because in many instances I know it is in the interest of the government and in the interest of the house to continue beyond ten o'clock. Therefore it should not become a practice to intrude government business into this period, and it must be recognized that ten o'clock means the hour of adjournment. If ten o'clock is definitely understood to be the hour of adjournment, and that we will not be very

Procedure Committee
literal in the interpretation of ten o'clock, then perhaps some of the difficulties might not arise. Therefore I wish to enter that caveat.
Second, I would have thought the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would have agreed on this point, which is one I do not want to propose as an amendment to the report, but which I hope will meet with his agreement. In paragraph 5, in the first line, I would have preferred to have seen after the word "with" the words "and subject to the limitations of standing order 39(1) as they apply to written questions and answers," so as to indicate clearly that the limitations which we have in our rules with respect to argument, opinion and so forth in regard to written questions should now apply also to oral questions.
I think Your Honour will agree with me that this is the most difficult area for the Chair in ruling as to whether questions are in the proper form and should be admissible or not. The same thing applies to answers. Standing order 39 is completely silent at present with regard to oral questions. It deals only with written questions on the order paper, but by tradition a similar right has grown up to ask oral questions and, by inference, that they should be guided by the rules which apply to written questions.
I would suggest it should be clearly set out that oral questions shall be subject to the same limitations as written questions and the same, of course, will apply to answers. I say this in order to strengthen the hand of the Chair in relying upon the precedents set by Your Honour's and my predecessors as to the nature and content of questions and answers.
The only way we can do it, and I am being legal in this, is by a reference to standing order 39(1), and if standing order 39(1) is not referred to in standing order 39(5), there could be an argument that all of these precedents and so forth had no application to oral questions. Therefore I hope it would be understood in this experimental period that the limitations in standing order 39(1) will apply to standing order 39(5).

I was fully aware of these suggestions by the committee, but I think this is a caveat with respect to the drafting of the standing order.
Perhaps I may refer to one other point, that is, the adjournment debate. It is intimated that an hon. member may give notice in writing of a question or a point which has risen during the question period and which he wishes to raise further. That is with respect to oral questions. I would point out that it is of equal importance that an hon. member should be able to raise a point in connection with the answer to a written question. Many of the difficulties which have arisen in the house have arisen out of the nature of a written reply which has led, in turn, to a question of privilege being raised, or ventilation of the subject matter under the guise of privilege. It is not really privilege, in my humble opinion. I feel this suggestion would be an improvement on the present arrangement and I commend it to hon. members. I appreciate that there is to be a six weeks trial period, but I think the house itself might be willing to accept this suggestion, that answers to written questions be included among those matters which can be discussed during the adjournment debate.

I am sure I am speaking for all hon. members when I say we are grateful to him and to his sub-committee for what they have done, and I think we can be glad that we have among us one with so much experience in this field as the hon. gentleman who presided over the sub-committee. We all, I think, appreciate the breadth of his knowledge in this field and the value of his experience. I may say its value would be even greater, of course, if by taking the appropriate action he could acquire some experience of rules and procedures from the vantage point of a place on this side of the house.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-on one side or the other, I hope to be able to speak with some authority in these matters. It seems to me that the report makes some interesting recommendations which may turn out to be of considerable value. It has been pointed out that if adopted they will be in effect for a trial period only to the end of May. I think this is a sensible way to proceed, because in the light of our experience we shall be able to decide whether to retain them, alter them, or drop them.
I find it very intriguing indeed to note from the report that an effort is being made to shorten the period devoted to questions without putting any time limit on the question period. That may well work out, Mr. Speaker, in the way the committee hopes it will, but I venture to express the hope, on my part, that it will not work out to the extent of our having to sit from 10 to 10.30 every night, because if that happens, and if we have the same length of time devoted to questions in addition to the extra half hour, we shall certainly not have expedited our proceedings. I know this is not in the minds of those who have made the recommendations in this report because it is pointed out with particular emphasis in the recommendation dealing with the shortening of the question period that the proceedings will have to be conducted along the lines indicated in paragraph seven of the report, that is to say oral questions will have to be governed by the rules laid down in subparagraph (c) of paragraph 7, they should only be in respect of questions of such urgency and importance as to require an immediate answer, and so forth, and also that answers to questions shall be as brief as possible to deal with the matter raised and should not provoke debate.
I would point out, however, that if an answer is not to provoke debate the question should not be of such a character as to be provocative and call for that kind of answer. If one is asked, for example: "What do you think about the European common market"
Procedure Committee
or "What do you think about the situation in Viet Nam?" it is difficult to be brief and to the point and not to provoke debate. I believe we shall have to practise a good deal of self-denial on both sides of the house. However, I am encouraged to think this may work, because one of the recommendations in the report says there may be no appeal against any ruling which you make, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this subparagraph. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that this means that once you have decided that a question is not in order there can be no appeal against your decision and that there can, surely, be no points of order or questions of privilege raised in respect to that decision. I say this because unless the word "appeal" is interpreted in this way we might waste as much time dealing with points of order and questions of privilege arising out of questions which have not been accepted by you, or accepted only for discussion at ten o'clock, as we would conceivably gain in other respects. Unless we interpret the recommendations in that way we might even find we have lost time rather than gained it.
I am interested in the recommendation dealing with a new procedure for handling notices of motion for the production of papers, a recommendation which I think should save time and expedite business. I say this because this is the first time, as far as I know, that a recommendation has been put forward containing the principle of an allocation of time to specific matters. In this case we are allocating a certain amount of time to debate on a particular subject, and that, I think, is of some significance.
On the whole we think these recommendations certainly deserve the trial they are to be given, and if they operate as the subcommittee hopes they will operate, they may be the first of a long series of recommendations from a very important committee which we have set up and which may go a long way toward making our House of Commons more effective in the discharge of the nation's business.
