subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The next time he objects to something I raised in the house I want Your Honour to remember that frank admission on the part of the Prime Minister. It was delightful, that admission, and one with which I am in entire agreement. The Prime Minister has referred to the committee and its operation. We have been trying through the years to bring about worth-while changes in the rules; committees have been set up and changes have been made. Further changes will have to be made. However, I should say this: I think you, Mr. Speaker, are the third or fourth Speaker who has headed a committee in this connection and I know that the house will agree that no one has given more devotion to making this chamber effective and assuring that the prerogative rights of parliament shall be maintained, while at the same time making those necessary alterations in the rules to meet changed and changing conditions. You have made a study of this subject and you have given a fine example in the chair of trying to carry out the embodiment of your views in this connection.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to point out, however, that in any changes made we must not deny parliament the fullest right of examination through questions. Some people say too many questions are asked. I read that in some sections of the press. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would recommend to those that hold that view an examination of the British Hansard where, in place of the few thousand questions that are asked here today, some 20,000 and more, as I recall it, are asked there. There one cannot rise and embarrass the government in any way by asking an initial question; the embarrassment always takes place in the subsequent questions, the supplementary questions that are asked.
Questions have their place and there must be no unnecessary interference with the full rights of members to ask such questions as come within the rules. There are many questions which could go on the order paper. However, I find that the order paper would indicate that a degree of celerity in the answering of questions has not always been characteristic of this government. I point out that according to computations made by another there are on the order paper 75 questions at this date that have been on the order paper for more than a month. There is something wrong if these questions cannot be answered. They are simple questions. The answers to some of them may not be as favourable to the government as it would like them to be; but there are more than

75 questions that have been on the order paper for more than a month. I am not going to read them.
Even worse is the fact that there are seven starred questions, questions that should be answered immediately, on the order paper which have been there for more than a month. The purpose of a starred question is to ensure that immediate attention be given to an immediate matter-and seven, as I said a moment ago, have been on the order paper for more than a month. Twenty eight questions have been on the order paper for three weeks and less. In the United Kingdom, when you ask a question it is answered within three days. That makes for an effective parliament. I am not speaking of starred questions now; starred questions are answered at the first opportunity, almost immediately. But other questions are answered within three days. I hope the spirit of co-operation that is apparent in the committee will find its way into the hearts of the ministers of the crown and that they will bring in answers to our questions expeditiously and without that delay that has so often characterized the answering of questions.
I am glad there has been the acceptance of a suggestion that I made, that where questions are not answered in a way that, in the opinion of the questioner, gives the full facts, an opportunity shall be available, within the limitations set out in the recommendation, to carry on beyond ten o'clock. The Prime Minister was a little concerned about this. I took it from his words that he thought it would really mean the house will be sitting from 10 to 10.30. You, Mr. Speaker, have seen the operation of the British parliament. I have seen it in operation, and sometimes when these questions arise, out of the 600 and some members of the House of Commons no more than three, four or five are in the chamber when these disputations take place following the regular adjournment hours of ten o'clock.
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is one that deserves the consideration of the committee. He pointed out that written questions, too, should be placed in the same category in so far as answers are concerned, so that anyone dissatisfied with such an answer would be able to raise the question, with Your Honour's leave, at the time of the automatic adjournment.
There is one suggestion that I make. It does not come within the purview of the report as it now is, but a reading of Hansard through the years indicates that interruptions from a seated position have become increasingly evident and the custom. When I first came here there were few of those;

one who wished to ask a question rose in his place. Today there are those seated interruptions. We are all guilty of them. It spoils the appearance of Hansard. It gives to readers of Hansard the idea that, to use a vulgarism, horseplay is indulged in by members from time to time. In my opinion, and I think the rules bear me out, no interruptions excepting those that are adopted by the person having the floor should find their way into Hansard. In the United Kingdom the course followed, after their experience of years in the mother of parliaments, is that when interruptions of this kind are made Hansard shows "An interruption", and that is all. The failure of Hansard to designate the member who made the interruption has a most salutary effect on the number of those interruptions. It is perhaps just a coincidence, but it is a fact with regard to an interruption or question asked. If there is no identification of the person making that interruption, it is surprising the degree to which that fact has an ameliorating effect on the enthusiasm of the interrupter.
As one looks at Hansard today one sees it plastered with questions and interruptions both at the time of questions prior to orders of the day and in general debate. One can only conclude that the acceptance of the principle I suggest, as followed in the mother of parliaments, would be beneficial here. That of course does not mean that in committee of the whole, committee of supply and the like, interruptions like that should not take place. They there have their place. But I am referring to the interruptions that consist of gratuitous statements made for no other purpose than to cause disruption, to disseminate humour, or for some other ulterior purpose.
I think the committee has done well in the recommendations already made; I think there is much more to be done. However, all the rules in the world will not bring about an expeditious and effective parliament without the co-operation of all of us, and I am sure that each of us personally will want to advise you of his or her intention to try to the limit to carry out the spirit of this house.
When people speak of the house being disorderly, I can only say to those who have come to that view that they know not Westminster. We had a visitor recently within the last two weeks, a professor of political science from the United States. I do not know the man but he is one of the outstanding political scientists in the eastern United States. He sat here in the gallery, and he said: "I want you to know and to let your fellow members in the House of Commons know that while I read of much criticism of the operation of your House of Commons I have found it a place of great dignity as compared to another 20220-150
Procedure Committee
representative institution"-which I am not going to identify. I hope that, as the Prime Minister said, we will be able, in that spirit of co-operation which you, sir, brought to parliament, to bring about in your period of office the greatest improvements in parliamentary procedure which have been made in a lifetime.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because I cannot make any claims to having had years of experience in this house-although I have had some experience in the way of getting things done as far as jobs which have come my way to do are concerned-and also because it is now two hours and 15 minutes since we began today's session and have not yet reached the question period, my remarks will be very brief. I commend the committee for the report they have submitted. I commend it to the house and suggest that we give it a fair trial. If we can all apply a little common sense and self-discipline I am sure that we will have a more effective House of Commons.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, personally, I have only two years' experience in parliamentary procedure. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I have yet to get the experience of those members who sit on the other side of the house, but I may have to my credit one experience more than he has.
It happened two week ends ago when the secondary school students in my riding asked me, Mr. Speaker-can you imagine that-to act as speaker in their mock parliament.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It must have been quite a task.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is exactly why I found the assignment very tough. I could not say a word during the two days that this mock parliament sat. However, it was good experience.
It also makes one realize the difficulties facing the man presiding over the proceedings of the house and what are his responsibilities.
For the suggestion made to us today to be successful, I think that first of all, the question askers should show good will, that those who have a question to ask should abide by the standing order established by the committee on procedure. That is of prime importance. The same goes for the ministers' answers.
Of course, we are doing this on a trial basis. But if all the answers given by the ministers bring about a request from the opposition to put on the agenda of the ten o'clock period the matter on which information is sought, it will not take a month before there are many more questions to discuss

Procedure Committee
during the period from ten to ten thirty on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays than all the questions or measures the government might want to introduce.
So, if the answers given by the ministers are ad hoc answers to the questions posed, there will be less disagreement on the experiment we want to try today.
But I think the greatest responsibility- and that is why at the outset of my remarks I said the Speaker had great responsibilities, for having experienced it myself-in this experiment will rest on the shoulders of the Speaker. It will be quite easy for him to rule that any question is out of order-there will be no point of order, no question of privilege. It will be the easy way.
It will be up to the Speaker also to decide which questions are urgent and which are not. In that connection, I should like to recall personal impressions in order to show that a question may seem urgent to some persons and not to others. When we first came to the house and listened to questions being asked concerning agriculture, all of them were accepted if they referred specifically to wheat; in such a case, they were urgent and important. However, if these questions referred to eastern agriculture, to the culture of potatoes, to stock breeding, to milk production or to something else, then they were ruled not urgent, and that seemed to be taken for granted by all parties in the house.
I will admit that, for a year now, hon. members seem to have taken into account the fact that certain matters which in former years did not seem to be urgent are very much so today.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that the most important point in this new experiment will be to determine which questions are urgent and important.
I should like to add a last point, mentioned earlier by the Leader of the Opposition, and it is this: questions on the order paper will have to be answered much sooner than has been the case till now. In respect of certain questions, we have had to wait a month, sometimes a month and a half, before getting an answer. That is why hon. members ask questions and request information on orders of the day instead of putting their questions on the order paper. If replies were provided sooner to questions put on the order paper, hon. members would be encouraged to use that media since such replies are more elaborate and, therefore, provide better information than those given during the question period. Indeed, that is quite understandable since the minister to whom the question is directed is then in a better position to get the necessary information and he can provide a more satisfactory reply when he has the time to prepare

himself than when a question is put to him without notice during the question period.
As far as our group is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we intend to co-operate loyally and sincerely in this new attempt, with a view to shortening the question period and expediting any legislation which might be more urgent. In fact, this constitutes the primary purpose of hon. members' work, that is to pass legislation which will serve the best interests of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just take a minute briefly to refer to one or two matters which have been introduced, bearing in mind that I did second this motion. First of all, I agree with what was said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that this house does not exist entirely for the purpose of permitting the business of government to be proceeded with; it also exists for the benefit of members of parliament to deal with grievances and matters of urgency affecting this country.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the situation in the old country. It so happens that I have before me a book entitled "Questions In Parliament" by Chester and Bowring. In order to emphasize what the Leader of the Opposition said I would point out that I find in the book that in 1945-46 there were 21,135 starred questions asked and a total of 27,313 starred and unstarred questions. In 1959-60 there were 10,161 starred questions asked and a total of 13,471 starred and unstarred questions. This indicates the extreme importance of this issue.
May I say that when the members of the subcommittee met we were as far apart as we could possibly be as to the type of amendments we should propose, and it was only by each accepting a little of the philosophy of the other and by reducing to some extent those things which we thought were essential that we were able to come up with this temporary measure which I think is going to be very effective in its operation. Finally, I should like to refer to the matters which were raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West. He brought up suggestions which I placed before the subcommittee and the committee. But I put it to you this way, Mr. Speaker. If we concur in this report we will then be saying by a vote of the house, because this will be a resolution passed by the house and it will become a part of the procedure, that we are accepting the guide lines and the suggestions as to questions and answers contained

in paragraph 7 of the committee's report. We are thereby saying that this is the view of the members of the house. We are asking you Mr. Speaker, in accordance with these guide lines to interpret what are questions of urgency, to designate the questions which should be asked and, just as important, to designate the type of answer which should be given pursuant to what we have set out in paragraph 7 of our report.
So, Mr. Speaker, while it might have been desirable from the viewpoint of neatness and tidiness to have incorporated this and the reference to standing order 39 (1) as a part of the new standing order, nevertheless by adopting the report we are in effect doing precisely that. We are in effect saying to you, sir, and to all members of the house: These are the rules which we as a body are directing and requesting each individual member to observe. Under those circumstances I feel that this procedure will be just as effective as if we had proceeded in the other way.
Motion agreed to.

I should like to make a short statement at this point. It is now five o'clock and so far as the Chair knows or its advisers, this is the first time it has happened that we are still on starred questions. The rules and standing orders are quite definite, it seems to us, and without unanimous consent of the house we must proceed to private members business at this time. If the house would grant me one minute, I should like to put on the record my reason for reaching this conclusion.
Our procedures at five o'clock are governed by a standing order which cannot be varied except by unanimous consent. Section (3) of standing order 15 provides that private members notices of motion must be taken on Mondays at five o'clock. On the other hand, section (4) of the same standing order provides that when a debate on a supply motion is in progress at five o'clock, the order for private members business would be suspended. The principal purpose of standing order 56 in my opinion is that it limits to two days a supply motion, while at the same time, ensuring, if possible, that no other proceedings shall intercept or impose themselves on the proceeding of a supply motion. However, it must be considered that the general ruling governing the proceeding at five o'clock is section (3) of standing order 15, and that section (4) of the standing order provides for a specific exception thereto which, in my opinion, must be so interpreted. Therefore, I have come to the conclusion that unless unanimous consent is granted, the house must proceed with private members business at this time.

speechtext:
This is the first supply motion in a series of six allowed by the rules for this session and we welcome the opportunity to draw some matters to the attention of the government and of the public. May I express the hope that the succeeding supply motions will be spaced out over the session as was the normal practice for many years in this house until last fall when five of them were crowded together for five successive weeks which, in effect, destroyed the value of supply motions to a certain extent.
The opposition is not suffering from any dearth of subjects to bring forward on supply motions, because when you have a government in retreat for a full year there are plenty of questions which need to be discussed, and discussed openly here in the House of Commons. I was impressed by the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) today when he advocated more open methods as being, to use his words, much better than the back room style of carrying on discussions and when he suggested that it is useful for public opinion to be brought more fully to bear on public matters. Here we have an opportunity on a supply motion to have an open discussion and in particular to bring to bear on important questions the weight of public opinion. My hope is that after this debate today and tomorrow the government will again retreat from the position it has taken.
I do not intend to adopt, as the Prime Minister used to do when he was leader of the opposition, a shotgun approach to a supply motion, that is to say, ramble all over the field and then, finally, under pressure, come down to one specific subject. I intend to announce within a few seconds, the subject matter that I have for discussion-a specific problem which I think should be dealt with by the House of Commons. And if the press of the country and the other news media adopt the suggestion of the Minister of Transport recommending analytic reporting of parliamentary proceedings we shall get across to the public of Canada this very important subject, and we shall have their opinion to reinforce the opinions of members of the House of Commons.
In order to relieve members of the cabinet from their worry-each one of them is-

speechtext: Trembling?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
-bothered by his conscience, I suppose, by something which has been going on in his department, something which he does not wish to have disclosed-in order to

Veterans Hospitals Transfer relieve those worried faces across this chamber I will say that the subject matter with which I am about to deal has to do with veterans affairs.
I am sure the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) who must have been anticipating I would raise this subject will be pleased to have the support of his colleagues, because collective responsibility is laid upon the members of the cabinet. I am sure all members of the cabinet from the Prime Minister down will give their close attention to this particular subject. Why has this subject come up for discussion? It has come up for discussion because over a period of almost three months we have been asking questions from this side of the house, attempting to get answers on this subject. Unfortunately, those answers have been ambiguous. They have obscured the issue and they have failed to give us the information which we sought. At least 18 questions have been asked on orders of the day in this chamber having to do with this problem, and when that number of questions is asked-and they were questions of urgency which would have been allowed even under the new rule we have adopted- the subject is one which obviously requires the attention of the government. That attention has not been given in a satisfactory way to this problem of veterans affairs.
Let us first consider the situation as far as veterans are concerned so that we may have some of the facts in front of us. I would refer to the committee report for 1962-63 which on page 79 indicates that there are in this country 150,724 disability pensioners-slightly over 40,000 from the first world war and some 106,000 from the second world war. The others are from Korea and the regular forces. So this is not a small problem from the standpoint of the disability pensioners, and the disability pensioners in 99 per cent of the cases are men who have been wounded. There are 150,000 of them in Canada.
Veterans of the first world war number about 40,000 and the disability pensioners are dying off at the rate of 2,000 a year. They belong to a vanishing race and the problem as far as they are concerned will disappear. The 100,000 from the second world war are now in middle age and we hope they will be with us for a good many years to come. Even if there are no more wars, and that is what we hope, the problem of Canada's war veterans is not one to be lightly brushed aside. I have given the house these figures so that hon. members may have an idea of the number of veterans who are being looked after by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Many of these disability pensioners, men with war wounds, are admitted to our veterans hospitals month after month and year after year.


Their cases come up for re-examination. As the years go by, deterioration sets in and a serious injury suffered in wartime many years ago, apparently healed, comes back to trouble the pensioner in later life.
In addition to those who are suffering from war wounds there are those who are on the war veterans allowance roll, and page 94 of the report indicates that there were 79,820 such people at the end of the fiscal year 196263. These are people, generally over 60 years of age, who are entitled to hospital treatment under the Department of Veterans Affairs. So that you have over 200,000 veterans of the first and second world wars and the Korean war who are entitled to treatment under the Department of Veterans Affairs, largely in the veterans hospitals. Some of them are looked after in other hospitals, but not very many.
There has been quite a bit of misinformation scattered here and there across the country as to the situation of the veterans hospitals. They are 11 in number. The beds available are roughly between 8,000 and 9,000; I believe 8,623 is the figure given in the departmental report. The occupancy figure is 80 per cent generally across the country, which I have been told is a reasonable occupancy figure. The admissions, people coming in, staying for a while and going out, for the fiscal year 1962-63 reached the total of 75,860, which gives you some idea of the tremendous load that is placed upon our veterans hospitals and the medical staffs which look after them. The average length of stay of those who come and go is slightly over 21 days. Then you have to consider how these people are divided up. In the report of the veterans affairs committee which sat last session, on page 372 you have the statement of the director of medical services for the department, who indicated in the first instance that there had been a decline in the number of hospital beds for our veterans. In 1945 there were 12,000; now it is down to roughly 8,600. So there has been a steady decline there. He divides into four categories, those people who are making use of the hospitals and are using the accommodation in the hospitals; those who are suffering from war wounds-the disability pensioner-15 per cent; those who are in the hospitals because of their entitlement under the War Veterans Allowance Act, 20 per cent. With regard to those who are in the hospitals because they need domiciliary care, I might just read what he says:
Fifty per cent of our hospital population is made up of people under section 29, this means people who are receiving domiciliary care.

He goes on to say:
I think that "domiciliary care" is a most unfortunate term because the fact is that these people in our hospitals are sick. They all have some degree of medical reason for being in the hospital and many of them have a very great degree of medical reason. They are bedridden, they need a great deal of chronic nursing care.
The balance of 15 per cent is made up of 6 per cent from the armed forces or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, 1 per cent patients receiving care at the request of other federal departments, and the rest are veterans who, although not entitled under the act to receive treatment in veterans hospitals, have been admitted and are paying their way for that treatment.
That gives you an idea of the problem which the Department of Veterans Affairs faces. I will not go into detail with regard to the history of our veterans hospitals, but it is a long and honourable history. It dates right back to the end of the first world war, and Canada has become accustomed now for 40 years to having our veterans looked after in separate institutions. Although at times there is here and there an individual who has some complaint with regard to his treatment in a veterans hospital, by and large the work in those veterans hospitals has been of a very, very high standard and has been satisfactory. Men who have been wounded, men who are on war veterans allowance, the aged and the infirm have been looked after in our veterans hospitals, and their relatives and friends have been very grateful for that assistance.
How has it come about that at this time we are facing an attack on our veterans hospitals? There are people who say, "Oh, well, we do not need to pay so much attention to our veterans". I will deal with this a little later on. There are those who are saying, "Well, some of the veterans should not be in those hospitals". Others say, "There are wards vacant, and they should be filled". This is all part of the general problem of hospital care for our population, and it is rather distressing if anywhere in the country there are wards in hospitals not utilized for the general population. One of the problems that the Department of Veterans Affairs faces, and has faced now for a number of years, is to get adequate staff in order to man completely the hospitals for which it is responsible. If the present Minister of Veterans Affairs can solve that problem, he has my good wishes, because I was faced with it during the time I held that portfolio. I refer to the problem of getting staff in order that no wards remain vacant in any veterans' hospital. But this is not an easy task and 1 am sure the department is working hard at that job right now.
Veterans Hospitals Transfer However, the general public looking at the situation, sometimes getting reports that are not completely factual, has gained the impression in some areas that the veterans do not require the care that they are now getting in the veterans hospitals, so that there is vacant space which should be made available to other members of the population, or something like that. I think any reasonable person would say that as our veteran population declines and vacant space becomes available in the present veterans hospitals, that space of course should be made available to others in the community who require medical attention. I think no one objects to that point of view. Contrary to an editorial in one newspaper, there is no "dog in the manger" attitude on the part of any veteran with regard to the veterans hospitals. As space becomes available, it should be placed at the disposal of others within the community who require hospitalization.
I have pointed out the burden which still weighs upon Canada for her present veteran population, and this cannot just be brushed aside easily. There are 200,000 veterans entitled under the act to receive treatment in our veterans hospitals. We cannot overlook the fact that the second world war veterans now approaching middle age will find increasing difficulties as the years go by. It is unfortunately true that as the years go by you do not just naturally recover from all the problems that affected you in your youth. On page 63 of the annual report there are some paragraphs worthy of note. The paragraph headed "Disabled veterans" reads:
There is a continuing need for special services to disabled veterans. Eighteen years of experience-
-this is since the second world war-
-have demonstrated to the satisfaction of the department that the war disabled can meet the challenge of normal peacetime living and make a substantial contribution to the economy of the country. Unfortunately, with the passing of the years, many wartime disabilities are being aggravated by the hazards and stress of modem living... As a result of these situations, there is a small but steady stream of veterans seeking advice and assistance with their problems of health and employment.
Then it goes on to say that during the last year 300 new disabled cases were registered for service. In the same period another 400 closed cases were reopened for service in specific areas of need. So it is not the type of work that can be called to a halt at any given moment.
Then at the bottom of the page there is a paragraph with regard to the older veterans: Any consideration of the welfare of older veterans invariably involves the services provided for the rehabilitation of the disabled and for this reason the branch has decided that its programs for assisting disabled and older veterans should be combined in one operational division. As world

Veterans Hospitals Transfer war II veterans are now of an average age of 45 years, it becomes apparent that all veterans may soon be classed as older veterans and the incidental demands for health and support due to age are bound to increase.
Everyone, of course, knows this.
Unfortunately, the process of ageing brings on many diseases and crippling conditions which force older veterans to retire from the employment market.
The point I am making is that it is a continuing problem. The number of veterans in this country is very large. As they get older the problem does not disappear. The first world war veterans will vanish, they will fade away; but the second world war veterans are here for years to come. Under these circumstances, what do you do with the veterans hospitals? When we had the opportunity of forming the government we asked the Glassco commission, in the midst of its manifold duties, to report on the veterans hospitals. This the Glassco commission did. I will not read at length what they reported, but they did look into the problem and make five recommendations, and I think that these five recommendations should be set out now, because I am laying the groundwork for subsequent speeches by my colleagues who will fill in other aspects of this problem. These are the five recommendations, which appear on page 195 of volume 3.
1.	No further hospitals be constructed by the government as active treatment hospitals for war veterans.
2.	Progressively, the treatment of veterans with pensionable disabilities be transferred to public hospitals, with the cost borne by the federal government.
3.	Veterans with major pensionable disabilities, who require chronic or domiciliary care, continue to be a federal responsibility.
4.	Veterans without major pensionable disabilities now receiving chronic and domiciliary care at public expense be progressively transferred to community facilities under such financial arrangements as may be expedient.
5.	Active treatment hospitals now operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs, when cleared, be sold and converted into community hospitals under transfer agreements providing preferential admission rights for veterans with pensionable disabilities.
That volume of the report was first brought to our attention in January, 1963. Immediately the prime minister of that day, the present Leader of the Opposition, was asked about it. The Montreal Gazette reports on January 9, 1963 his reaction to that report as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker said pointedly yesterday that he "disagreed" with some features of report No. 3 released on Monday night.
Mr. Diefenbaker singled out the veterans hospitals proposal as one which was "rather more sweeping than I think the government would give acceptance to".

"I don't know how my colleagues feel but I would not agree with that recommendation," he said-
I was in Winnipeg when I was asked for my reaction, which is quoted in the same paper. I was not in consultation with the then prime minister but I issued a statement which is reported in the Gazette as follows:
"No steps will be taken at this time to change in any way the present care and treatment of our veterans", veterans affairs minister Churchill said in Winnipeg.
"Newspaper accounts appear to me to have exaggerated some of the recommendations of the report", Mr. Churchill said.
"I want to assure all veterans in our hospitals, and all others who are interested, that no steps will be taken to change in any way the present care and treatment of our veterans at the present time".
"The distinction between active treatment and chronic care treatment is very well known to the department and has been the subject of very intense study by the department and myself during the last two years. Plans for chronic care and treatment to release active treatment beds are very far advanced, and decisions thereon were deferred pending the report of the Glassco commission.
"The suggestion that a $200,000,000 expenditure on hospital construction has been contemplated for the future is without any foundation to my knowledge".
"The care and treatment of Canada's veterans is a major obligation of this country which has been, and will continue to be, thankfully borne by Canada because of the sacrifices made by Canadian servicemen in wartime, and so long as I am minister of veterans affairs or have any government responsibility for veterans affairs, there will be no change in the care and treatment of our veterans unless it is clearly and unmistakably for their benefit".
In the same issue of the Montreal Gazette Judge C. C. Sparling, president of the Royal Canadian Legion, is reported as follows:
In Winnipeg, Judge C. C. Sparling, president of the Royal Canadian Legion, had described the recommendation that veterans hospitals be closed down as "shocking". He said that he was convinced that the Glassco commission's call for a revision of this and other services offered to Canadian veterans would be received with "grave misgivings" by the nation's 1,500,000 war veterans.
That was our response to the Glassco commission report. We went further than that and said: "Hands off the veterans hospitals". That has been our stand ever since and there has been no interference with the veterans hospitals. Repeatedly I have said to those who have asked me about it that there is no haste in this matter. The problem is very great at the present time. Several years will have to elapse before the burden of looking after war veterans has decreased; and I have given you the figures as of today where there are over 200,000 entitled to treatment in our hospitals, with thousands who may require treatment as the years go by-because there were one million people in uniform in the second world war.

In my opinion the Glassco commission report failed to appreciate the problem of veterans hospitals, although a great part of the report, which was voluminous and comprehensive and extended over five volumes, was acceptable and is being put into effect by the government. But so far as veterans hospitals are concerned I think the Glassco report was wrong. 1 think those who wrote that particular section of it failed to understand the problem.
I have set these facts before the house and I now want to deal with the attitude of the present government. I have given our stand concerning veterans hospitals and we have not changed our stand. We appreciate the problem. I appreciated it when I was minister of veterans affairs. We were waiting for the Glassco commission report before a final decision was made and it was just after the report was made that I was transferred to another department. Then the government changed and consequently there has perhaps been some delay.
We were quite aware of the fact that our veterans hospitals contain a number of veterans who do not require active treatment. We did not have in mind the building of new and expensive hospitals and running up a bill of $200 million. That is simply ridiculous. I have no idea where the Glassco commission got that figure. We had no such idea at all. One or two hospitals needed renovating. There may perhaps be one new building required but the enlarging of the number of active treatment veterans hospitals was not in contemplation.
We were considering what to do with those people who do not require active treatment accommodation but rather care somewhat similar to what can be had in a nursing home. In that regard there are examples of satisfactory operations which are going on under the Department of Veterans Affairs in Vancouver, Saskatoon and Ottawa where older people who are still mobile are looked after because they require a certain amount of medical supervision and nursing care.
All this information is available to the department. We took the stand that we were not going to swallow the Glassco commission report, hook, line and sinker, without a thorough study of it. I had hoped that the present government would do the same. However, that is not the case. We heard rumours about changes being made and a whole series of questions was put to the Minister of Veterans Affairs earlier in the session. After considerable delay he finally produced a statement on March 16. He wanted to smuggle it into Hansard. He was not going to read it. He wanted it printed as an appendix. But the Leader of the Opposition 20220-151
Veterans Hospitals Transfer (Mr. Diefenbaker) very properly asked him to read it and so it is recorded on page 929 and subsequent pages of Hansard. His statement sets out the policy of the government with regard to veterans hospitals. As found on page 930 he said:
Consequently the only practical solution to the very real problem we face is to enter into agreements with suitable agencies to take over the operational control of veterans hospitals. These would then become general community hospitals, in which the department could purchase the service it must provide.
As found on page 931 he summed up the matter in these words:
It is therefore the view of this government that the operational control of veterans hospitals should be transferred to non-federal agencies at times, in places, and under conditions which will best protect the standards of care to which veterans are entitled.
On March 26 I sought an assurance from the minister. As found on page 1497 of Hansard I said:
Will the minister give an assurance to this house that no hospital under the control of the veterans affairs department will be transferred to other authorities until the matter has been discussed and approved by parliament?
The minister thought that was a very involved question and, after an exchange of questions and answers, he went on to say:
-as to submitting the matter and debating it before parliament in each instance, I think the hon. gentleman will realize this is an impossible thing to do because it would require or may require 11 or 12 different submissions to cover each instance.
In other words, he was contemplating the transfer of the 11 hospitals. Then I said:
I take it we now have the assurance of the minister that he intends to transfer the veterans hospitals to other authorities. Is that correct?
The minister replied:
The statement I made in the house the other day was, I think, quite clear-
The statement made the other day was, I presume, his statement of March 16, the operative sections of which I have just read. Not content with that, in addition to questions asked by other members the hon. member for Middlesex West asked the Prime Minister a question supplementary to one I had asked on March 30 last. As found on page 1544 of Hansard the hon. member used these words:
Can the Prime Minister assure the house that if arrangements are made to let other interests use some of the hospital beds now under the control of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the actual control of these hospitals will be left with the Department of Veterans Affairs?
The Prime Minister replied:
I think it would be the intention, Mr. Speaker, that the hospitals be left in the control of the department.

Veterans Hospitals Transfer
I suggest that we pause there to reflect on what those words meant. I took them to mean that in the mind of the Prime Minister there would be no transfer of the hospitals from the control of the department, if words carry the clear meaning that seems to be contained in those words. I subsequently asked him if he had not given a different answer to me than he gave to the hon. member for Middlesex West, but he said I was not using quite the same words I had used in my earlier question.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I will continue at eight o'clock.

maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF HOSPITALS FROM FEDERAL CONTROL
speechtext:
At six o'clock I was drawing attention to the statements which were made in the house by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) which were contrary one to the other. I quoted from Hansard of March 16 where the minister made a statement; March 26, when I tried to get assurances from him that there would be no transfer of veterans hospitals; March 30, when the Prime Minister said he thought it would be the intention that the hospitals remain in control of the department. I would have thought when that was said by the Prime Minister the issue would have been settled and the Minister of Veterans Affairs would have immediately informed the house that no change would be made. He remained unconvinced by the Prime Minister's statement and this is what makes it so difficult in this house. Where do we place our reliance? We get one answer from a minister and a different answer from the Prime Minister. Which one do we believe?
Well, for the time being, I guess we have to rely on the Minister of Veterans Affairs, because after that statement by the Prime Minister the Minister of Veterans Affairs was out in Winnipeg during the first week of April. The Winnipeg Tribune of April 4 reports in part as follows:
He-
This is referring to the Minister of Vet-rans Affairs.
-admitted there would be some uncertainty and difficulties during the transition period when the hospitals changed control.
Obviously, he had in his mind that the hospitals would change control, and that is the impression that he left with the people of Winnipeg. This is what I have heard with


regard to his meeting out there and his interview on CJOB, as well as his interview with the press. On April 8, after his return, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh), as recorded at page 1915 of Hansard, asked this question:
Is it the intention of this government to turn over the veterans hospitals to the provincial authorities?
The minister answered as follows:
-if we can be satisfied that we shall be given the necessary safeguards and guarantees so that veterans' rights will definitely be protected, it is our intention to proceed with it.
So there you have the story up to April 8, and the intention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs is to turn over the veterans hospitals to other authorities, either provincial or municipal. He mentioned certain safeguards which should be established. He says that this must be done in order to assure that the standard of treatment is maintained, and various things like that. Obviously, however, he is determined on his course. It has been impossible for the House of Commons to get a clear answer from the government in view of the somewhat evasive statement of the minister himself and in view of the statement of the Prime Minister which was the opposite to that made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what is the stand of veterans organizations on this question? The Royal Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations have been attempting to get a satisfactory answer from the minister, but have had no success. The standing committee on veterans affairs, when it met last session made the following recommendation, which is recorded on page 430 of the committee minutes, and I quote:
Your committee is aware that a point has been reached where a decision must be made regarding treatment services in both areas of responsibility and administration. Your committee recommends that fullest consultation be carried out with veterans organizations before any changes are made.
On March 16, when the minister made his statement to the house, he met with representatives of the Royal Canadian Legion afterwards, and not before. The Royal Canadian Legion issued a release the following day from which I will quote two paragraphs:
"The Royal Canadian Legion is opposed to any change in the D.V.A. treatment arrangements that will alter the present provisions for treatment of veterans under any of the classifications of the veterans treatment regulations" said Fred O'Brecht dominion 1st vice president.
Mr. O'Brecht was commenting on the statement made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs which outlined the proposed turnover of D.V.A. hospitals to municipalities or provincial governments.
After the representatives of the Legion had met with the minister, they wrote him a letter

dated March 20 and they issued a press release so that everybody would know the result of their meeting with the minister. In part, this press release reads as follows:

This question has been one of great

It is of concern to veterans generally and to their dependants, and I think it is of concern to a very large number of Canadians who recognize we have a particular responsibility toward the veterans of this country who defended it in two world wars and in other wars.
This is a subject which is very dear to my heart, personally, as I have a lot of friends among the veteran population in my own constituency and in other parts of Canada. I speak tonight as a member of this house after 19 years of experience on the veterans affairs committee, as the president of the 54th Kootenay battalion C.E.F., which was one of the finest battalions in the Canadian expeditionary force. As a man with a knowledge of veterans needs as a result of long association with them, and with a knowledge of their attitude toward veterans hospitals and their recognition of the services rendered by them to veterans since their inception. Generally speaking, veterans appreciate the high standard of service which has been given by veterans affairs hospitals. There is a certain possessiveness among veterans with regard to these hospitals throughout Canada; they feel they are their own hospitals, and when, unfortunately, they have to enter these hospitals as they grow on in years they meet comrades who, perhaps, fought in the same wars they did, sometimes in the same regiment, or brigade, or division. So there is a lot of sentiment attached to these hospitals as far as the veterans are concerned.
A debate like this revives memories, and when you get to be an old man like me you cannot help living in the past on occasion. When I discuss a subject like this I think of some of the men I knew. I think of the unusual characters. In the opinion of this party the veterans of Canada have a particular claim to consideration with respect to this question. I say that without any hesitation whatsoever. We did think it would have been understood-and this is what we hoped-that the policy would be devised as the result of the closest possible consultation with all the veterans organizations and then, possibly, further reference to the committee with, later, a co-operative drafting of policy to meet the needs of the present and protect the rights of veterans in this country. When you attend these branch meetings of veterans organizations, of Legions in my constituency in southeastern British Columbia, and the ladies auxiliaries meetings, you get a very good idea what the ordinary veteran is thinking on these questions.

I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have had a long association with veterans organizations and a long association with a large number of veterans. The very veterans legislation that we have on the statute books of this country, known as the veterans charter, is the result of the representations made by veterans organizations, consideration by committees and consideration by governments. I am sure that as far as Canada is concerned there have been none of the excesses that have been experienced in the United States on some occasions.
I think throughout the years they can be credited with being very responsible indeed, because they are good Canadians. They have a sensible approach to many of these problems. Throughout the years we have had

quite unusual and unexpected problems develop with respect to veterans legislation owing to changing circumstances, changing needs, changing times and all the rest. These problems have all been met in a very sound and satisfactory manner. We found that amendments were necessary from time to time in the principles of legislation, the amounts of pensions, war veterans allowances and so on, and governments have responded to these representations because they knew they were valid.
Our first duty, Mr. Speaker, is to protect the veterans in this respect. Therefore, we insist, first of all, that the service to veterans must be maintained at the present high standard of service, both to veterans suffering from acute illness or from chronic illness. Mind you, we have the veterans of the first world war, many of whom are getting on in years, and in many cases they require treatment for chronic conditions. A few are acute cases. Then we have the veterans of the second world war, and possibly the acute cases will start to rise for some time now and later we will have to provide further care for those who become chronic cases. We suggest that where there are empty beds and it is possible to meet local requirements, arrangements be made with local authorities to lease wings or floors of these hospitals which are available so as to provide for such local need. That is an aspect of the subject which warrants consideration by the department, by veterans organizations and by the provincial or municipal authorities particularly interested. Therefore, in the third place, I think that this whole question should be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs so that once again, in view of recent developments, we can hear the opinions of veterans organizations on this question.
Then, fourth, after the committee has met and has made its recommendations we suggest that there should be close consultation between the dominion command of veterans organizations and the Department of Veterans Affairs with regard to the whole problem. Then we will be able to lay down a general policy for the whole of Canada. Then, the department can meet with provincial or local branches to deal with any particular problem related to the area in which the
Veterans Hospitals Transfer branch is established. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), I will only say a few words about the organization of veterans' hospitals in Canada and about the government's decision not to relinquish its responsibilities but to entrust to others the duty of providing treatment to veterans.
We have much respect for veterans because most of them fought overseas. They served in the Canadian army and, personally, I remember that at the beginning and during the last war, Canadians were told: "Enlist in the Canadian army, fight for your country and you will never have any more trouble, and the conditions which led to this war will never recur. The government will look after you, your security and your family".
I knew various veterans who, when they came back from overseas or elsewhere, were bitterly disappointed to find out that the war once ended, the government, after having succeeded in obtaining an adequate fighting force, did not seem too interested in their welfare and in their security. Such attitude entailed much hardship for some who wanted to find employment. Indeed, I personally know able veterans who tried to find work in various government departments after the war. Of course, they were ready to give them a priority at the time, as it is still done today. But, on the other hand, the positions offered

Veterans Hospitals Transfer were so "non-specific", if you will, and the salaries so inadequate, that veterans had practically no protection at all from the federal government.
Therefore, those veterans had to find employment elsewhere and later to launch another campaign, not of a military character, but an economic and industrial campaign to earn their living.
And little by little, physical troubles resulting from action on the battlefields or from their military service began to show, and the veterans who thought that they were in good health realized one day that they were suffering from ailments which they attributed to their military service.
It is quite possible, I admit, that those discomforts might have been caused by their military service or that their ills were aggravated by their participation in combat, or still that this physical condition went unnoticed when they enrolled for military service. But, the result was that veterans started to insist on getting medical care in veterans hospitals because they were unable to have their degree of disability recognized and because the pension they received was not high enough. That is why there are so many veterans hospitals today. As a matter of fact, there was a rather sharp increase in such hospitals after the war because a great number of veterans required medical treatment.
While in theory those veterans could get an increased pension which would enable them to keep staying at home, to use their family life to rehabilitate themselves or even make a greater contribution to civilian life, because of those various reasons they feel they must go to those veterans hospitals to have at least free medical services provided by the government.
That deplorable situation is the result of a system which developed out of various economic and political conditions, so that those veterans have to take advantage of the services offered to them by veterans hospitals.
I do not think the government is justified in maintaining such a large and expensive qualified personnel to take care of a number of veterans which may not be large enough. And personally, I see no objection to the government entrusting someone else with the hospital and medical function, providing it has the assurance that the veterans will lose absolutely nothing in terms of hospital efficiency.
On that score, I should like to quote from the release issued last month by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet). That statement made by the minister indicates very clearly the conditions which will have to be accepted before the federal government

gradually withdraws from the administration of veterans' hospitals. Here is what the minister said, and I quote:

At this point I would like to make it unequivocally and emphatically clear that no such agreements will be entered into by the government unless certain sine qua non conditions are met. These conditions, three in number, are as follows: First, accommodation for the treatment of service connected disabilities among veterans must be immediately available at all times, and treatment must be provided in accordance with standards prescribed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Second, community institutions of acceptable standards must be available to look after the work load created by other classes of veterans, which means that such veterans will be able to obtain treatment in their own communities, near their own friends and families. Finally, satisfactory arrangements must be made for the continued employment of professional and other staffs now serving in our institutions.

What do we read, Mr. Speaker, in this statement by the Minister of Veterans Affairs? The veterans themselves, members of medical and hospital staff will not be prejudiced, because the department will make sure that this personnel will be sent where its services will be required. On the other hand, I think that the federal budget, for a definite period, will be relieved accordingly, since it is clear that there is at present a duplication of services which could be supplied somewhere else.
As I said, we must respect the rights of veterans to receive medical services. Also, we should not suggest that the staff was not efficient, on the contrary: the medical, hospital and nursing personnel in veterans hospitals is excellent; diagnostic and research facilities are excellent. However, there is a duplication of functions in most cases.
In my own riding there is a veterans hospital, l'Hopital des anciens combattants de Sainte-Foy, and in addition there is a hospital section coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence so that we have the hospital services of the Canadian Army and those of the veterans administration. In both hospitals, or at least in one, university teaching is carried out, which means that this is an important hospital, fully equipped to render the services expected from it. This means also that the medical students of the area can take advantage of its services. However, I do not think that it is because of the fact that there are veterans in that hospital that students can receive such teaching; it is rather on account of its good organization, good maintenance and because the department heads are qualified.
However, since in the majority of cases we are dealing with chronic patients, or at least with patients requiring indefinite treatment,

it turns out, in the long run, even at the teaching level, that the cases found there have lost a lot of their importance for the students and the medical faculty.
That is why as long as the requirements set out by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the government are met in the hospitals, I am personally convinced that the veterans in my constituency will be well looked after and that they will get in a very short space of time and without delay the same treatment as before.
I am convinced also that the members of the medical, hospital, social welfare nursing staff will be able to keep on practising in other fields which will have been accepted by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Personally, I am satisfied with such conditions and I believe that we should accept, in order to ensure greater efficiency, the new policy adopted by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I would not object either if it were submitted to the veterans affairs committee since that group was set up to study that department's problems. Everyone should have the opportunity to express his views, including members of national veterans' organizations and the Canadian Legion, for which we have great respect.
I feel that the main thing is to convince those who have contributed to the defence of our country and others that they can rest assured that we remember them and that, as we promised them before they joined up, we will never forsake them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has always been the tradition of this parliament to deal with veterans problems and matters affecting the welfare of veterans in a non-partisan manner. Certainly, during

Veterans Hospitals Transfer the 15 years I have been a member of this house I have never known any want of confidence motion seeking to divide the house on any matter pertaining to the welfare of veterans. I must confess that I am a little disappointed at the departure involved in the amendment which we have before us this evening. I am sure all hon. members subscribe to the philosophy that human beings are the most important things in this world. When we come to that particular class of human beings who have served their country, have fought, bled and sacrificed their limbs, I am sure we all feel that they should be placed in a preferred class. Next to them in preference would be their widows, orphans and dependants.
The objective of policy pertaining to veterans affairs over the years has been to find what is the very best that can be done for the veterans. This has been the objective of policy no matter what party has been in power. I feel sure that that objective remains today the very same as it has been down through the years.
When the first great war produced casualties Canada, as a grateful nation, assumed certain obligations toward her veterans. One of those obligations was treatment services. Those treatment services were, first, to repair as much as possible the ravages of war and, second, to provide medical treatment to the veterans for their disabilities resulting from service as long as they lived. This treatment commitment was written into the law for two specific groups of veterans. One group, of course, was the disability pensioner; the other group was the war veterans allowance recipient.
Now, some may hold the opinion that the disability pensioner has a stronger claim or perhaps a greater entitlement than the war veterans allowance recipient. Today, when we have more advanced knowledge of the effects of stress and tension, that theory may not stand up too well. But be that as it may, under the law both have the same entitlement. The law applies equally to each and imposes the same obligation on the government to provide treatment to each group of veterans.
In discharging these commitments this or any government is faced with certain problems. At present, and looking to the future, the chief problem appears to be the ability to maintain an adequate standard of treatment service. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who moved the amendment, admitted that this problem exists, so there is no reason why time should be used in belabouring that point.
However, in seeking for a solution to this particular problem we must face certain basic factors as they present themselves to us at present. These factors may change over the

years, but at present we must deal with them as we find them and as they are presented to us by our experts. The first of these basic factors is the shortage of doctors. I do not think there will be very much disagreement on that point. There is hardly any province that has an adequate supply of doctors. In fact in my own province the shortage is so great we have to try and induce medical men to come over from Great Britain and European countries.
The second basic factor that cannot be ignored is the class of patients who have to be treated. At present, and for some time past, 70 per cent of the patients being treated in veterans hospitals are war veterans allowance recipients. This situation will continue for a good many years, and the longer it continues the longer it will carry with it another problem, namely the increasing number of veterans requiring chronic care.
The third factor that must be considered is our constitutional position, because health services are really a provincial responsibility, and we know from experience that many provinces do not take kindly to the federal government encroaching on provincial prerogatives. We cannot ignore these three basic factors, and any solution we may find must take them into account.
I know veterans may say, "Why don't we open the doors of our veterans hospitals to civilian patients?" I think most veterans would be happy if that solution could be adopted, but we have advice that it is not quite that easy, and therefore we cannot brush off this constitutional position in which we find ourselves.
These factors I have mentioned vary in different parts of Canada and, not only do they vary, but there are other factors which vary as well. Consequently, as the minister has pointed out on many occasions in the house, there can be no over-all solution. We must take each problem, each situation separately, and work out a separate solution in the light of what can be accomplished under the prevailing circumstances.
The minister has made it clear that in seeking solutions certain guide lines will be followed and certain principles adopted to safeguard the interests of the veterans. He will be dealing with this tomorrow in more detail, and there is no need for me to take time now to develop this particular point.
There seems to be an idea abroad, and it is implied in the amendment before us, that the government intends to turn over all of its hospitals, in a wholesale manner, to non-D.V.A. agencies. Certainly that is not the situation as I understand it. On many occasions the minister has said that we would

have to deal with each case on its merits and at no time, to my knowledge, has anyone said that all the hospitals are going to be turned over to non-D.V.A. agencies.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether radio reports are correct that the government is now in full retreat from its announced intention to transfer the veterans affairs hospitals to other levels of government.
Now the Prime Minister comes into the picture. For three months or more this diplomacy was going on behind doors, but when they want to get a little publicity and make headlines they come out in front of the doors. The Prime Minister said: "No, Mr. Speaker". Then the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said: "Just partially". Then the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) said:

I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister supplementary to that of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Can the Prime Minister assure the house that if arrangements are made to let other interests use some of the hospital beds now under the control of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the actual control of these hospitals will be left with the Department of Veterans Affairs?
The Prime Minister replied:
I think it would be the intention, Mr. Speaker-
He does not say it will be the intention; he thinks it would be.
-that the hospitals be left in the control of the department.
I do not know whether the veterans are so concerned about that proposition. If control remains in the Department of Veterans Affairs, but the use of the hospitals for treatment purposes is made available to the provinces, I do not think the veterans are concerned about the word "control" in that sense. They want to retain control of this hospital for the use of veterans in southern Alberta and in the city of Calgary, not control in the sense that the department has title only to the hospital but has leased it to the province for the use of other people for the next 25 years.
There is the confusion, Mr. Speaker. There is the reason that the veterans are sending telegrams to all members of parliament asking them to try to smoke out the minister, find out what he meant by his statement, whether the Prime Minister meant what he said or whether the Minister of Veterans Affairs has contradicted the Prime Minister. We do not know what the policy is; it is so mixed up. The minister will come out with a statement wrapped up in beautiful language. That is what they call open diplomacy.

speechtext:
There is one thing I always like, a good chorus to a well played tune. The Prime Minister said:
I think it would be the intention, Mr. Speaker, that the hospitals be left in the control of the department.
Then the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister to clarify two conflicting answers he has given this afternoon. He indicated to me that the veterans hospitals would be transferred to other authorities, and he indicated to the hon. member for Middlesex West that it was not the intention of the government to do so. What is the situation?
Now he has smoked out the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has misinterpreted my answer to him, as I think he will find out when he reads Hansard.

I have read Hansard, Mr. Speaker; I have read it aloud in the House of Commons and I challenge anybody to say from that answer of the Prime Minister or from his answers on other occasions what the situation is. What is the policy? Is it to sublease these hospitals, to transfer them to the provinces or, in the case of Calgary, to transfer the hospital to the city of Calgary? The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Hays) should be in his place and should be concerned about the veterans of Calgary tonight. He should be the man to speak for that section of his constituency where the Colonel Belcher hospital is situated.
This is the situation. We have the Prime Minister saying one thing and the Minister of Veterans Affairs saying another thing. The Prime Minister says he does not think we are really going to transfer these hospitals and give title to the provinces. I take it from the answers of the Minister of Veterans Affairs which I have read that, not only are they going to give control to the provinces, but they are going to have the right to use them. What is the situation? This amendment has been moved because we have been asking for answers to our questions and have not received them.
Business of the House
I think the federal government should say to the province of Alberta: If you are in difficulty, like other provinces, with regard to a shortage of beds then it is your responsibility because since 1958 you have received $86 million from the federal government by way of assistance with regard to one category or another of hospitalization. If there is a shortage of beds it is the responsibility of the province. It is particularly their responsibility to complete University hospital in Calgary, where the steel structure has been standing unfinished for several years. Let us exert some pressure on the province to build that hospital. Then the province will not have to take over the veterans hospital.
I see it is now ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
